courses.title: How Machines Think
courses.tagline: Machines are not clever. They are just very, very good at following your rules.
courses.intro: You are about to find out the biggest secret in the world of computers: machines cannot think at all. They only sort, count, and follow steps — and you already know how to do all three. By the end of this course you will have taught a machine to see something with your own two hands.
courses.parentNote: Your child will learn what sorting, rules, patterns and training data really are, using stones, caps and cardboard before ever touching a screen. By module 8 they can train a simple image recogniser on a shared phone and explain, out loud, exactly why it works and where it fails.

modules.title: Sorting Is Thinking
modules.bigIdea: Every clever machine starts with one simple move: putting things that are alike into the same pile.

seeThis.caption: Two piles on the ground: stones on one side, leaves on the other. Nothing else.

youNeed: about 20 stones and 20 leaves, mixed in a heap
a flat patch of ground or floor
a stick to draw a line
doThis: Draw one long line in the dust with your stick. Left side, right side.
Mix your stones and leaves into one messy heap. Really mix them.
Now sort. Stones left, leaves right. Do it as fast as you can while someone counts.
Say the rule out loud: 'If it is hard, go left. If it is soft, go right.' That sentence is the whole thing.
Point at your two neat piles. That picture is what a machine makes inside itself, every single time.
Now try a mean trick: put in one dry, hard leaf. Which pile? Argue about it with someone.
modules.whyItWorks: A sorting machine has no eyes and no opinions. It has a rule, like 'hard goes left', and it follows that rule on every single thing you hand it. The dry hard leaf is the interesting part — real machines get confused by exactly that kind of in-between thing, and people who build them spend most of their time on those.
modules.challenge: Sort the same heap again but with a brand new rule — by size, or by colour. Can a friend guess your rule after watching you sort only five things?

words.means: to put things into groups that belong together
the one sentence you follow every time, no exceptions

modules.title: Be the Robot
modules.bigIdea: A machine only does what you said — not what you meant.

seeThis.caption: A friend standing frozen, waiting for the next command, with a bucket on the ground ahead.

youNeed: one friend, brother or sister willing to be the robot
a bucket, tin or cup placed across the room or yard
chalk or a stick
doThis: Your friend is now a robot. Robots do NOTHING unless told. No thinking allowed.
Before they move, say every step out loud: 'Take four steps forward. Turn right. Take two steps. Bend down. Close hand.'
Run it. The robot must do exactly what you said — if you forgot 'bend down', they must grab at the air.
When it goes wrong, do not fix it by talking. Go back and change your list of steps, then run it again.
Keep fixing until the robot lifts the bucket. Then say your whole list out loud in one breath. That list has a name: an algorithm.
Swap places. Now you be the robot and feel how annoying a bad list is.
modules.whyItWorks: This is exactly what programming feels like. The computer is not being difficult — it is being perfectly obedient to instructions that were slightly wrong. Every programmer in the world spends their day doing what you just did: running the steps, watching them fail, and fixing the list.
modules.challenge: Write an algorithm for making tea, then make a grown-up follow it word for word. Try not to laugh when they pour water on the closed cup.

words.means: a list of steps in order, like a recipe
a step that is missing or wrong, so things go funny

modules.title: Guess My Rule
modules.bigIdea: A machine learns by looking at lots of examples until it can guess the rule by itself.

seeThis.caption: Rows of bottle caps, some rows with a tick beside them, some with a cross.

youNeed: a big handful of bottle caps in two or three colours
a friend
ground to lay them out on
doThis: One of you invents a secret rule and tells nobody. Something like 'a row is good if it has a red cap in it'.
The rule-keeper lays out a row of caps and says only 'good' or 'not good'. No explaining.
Do this ten times. Keep the good rows on the left and the not-good rows on the right so you can see them all at once.
The guesser now stares at the two groups and lays out a brand new row, saying 'I think this one is good'.
Rule-keeper answers only yes or no. Keep going until the guesser gets five right in a row.
Now say the rule out loud. Were you right? Look at how many examples it took.
modules.whyItWorks: You just did machine learning. Nobody told the guesser the rule — they worked it out from examples marked good and not-good. That is exactly how a phone learns to spot a diseased cassava leaf: thousands of leaf photos, each one marked sick or healthy, until the machine can guess the rule on a leaf it has never seen.
modules.challenge: Make a rule so sneaky it takes your friend twenty examples — but it must still be a real rule you can say in one sentence. No cheating by changing it halfway.

words.means: one thing you show the machine, with the answer attached
to work out the rule by looking at many examples

modules.title: Teach the Phone to See
modules.bigIdea: You can train a real machine to recognise something today, with a borrowed phone and thirty photos.

seeThis.caption: A phone screen with two rows of photos: a row of mangoes, a row of bananas, each row labelled.

youNeed: one shared phone with a browser and internet, even for 20 minutes
two kinds of object with about 15 of each — mangoes and bananas, or stones and leaves
good daylight, not a dark room
doThis: On the phone browser, open a free 'teach the computer to see' training page (Google's Teachable Machine works and needs no login).
Make Class 1. Point the camera at your mangoes and hold the record button while you turn them around. Get about 30 pictures.
Make Class 2. Do the same with the bananas. Same light, same background — this matters more than you think.
Press Train. Wait. It takes less than a minute. Something just changed inside that phone.
Hold up a mango it has never seen. Watch the bar jump to 'mango'. That bar moving is your proof — point at it.
Now hold up your own hand. Watch it guess wrongly and confidently. Laugh, and remember it for module 6.
modules.whyItWorks: The phone never learned what a mango is. It learned which patterns of colour and shape were in the pictures you labelled 'mango'. That is why it still answers when you show it your hand — it must pick one of the two boxes you gave it, so it picks the closest. Real farm apps that spot sick cassava leaves are built the exact same way, just with far more photos.
modules.challenge: Train it on your face versus your friend's face. Then try to fool it with a hat, a hand over one eye, or standing in shadow. How many tricks did it take?

words.means: to show a machine many labelled examples so it can guess later
the name you attach to an example, like 'mango'

modules.title: The Bot That Talks Back
modules.bigIdea: A talking machine is just a big pile of 'if they say this, answer that'.

seeThis.caption: A cartoon character on a phone screen with a speech bubble answering a greeting.

youNeed: the shared phone with a block-coding site open (Scratch or similar)
a quiet corner so you can hear it
paper to plan your answers first
doThis: On paper first: write five questions people ask you, and the answer for each. This paper IS your program.
In the block editor, drag an 'ask and wait' block so your character asks 'What is your name?'.
Add a 'say' block that greets them back using the answer. Run it. Your name appears in the bubble — point at it.
Now add an 'if' block: if the answer is 'good', say something happy; otherwise say something kind.
Add three more if-blocks from your paper list. Run the whole thing with a friend typing.
Ask it something you never wrote a block for. Watch it say nothing, or say the wrong thing.
modules.whyItWorks: Your bot feels alive for about four questions, then falls apart — because it has no idea what words mean. It only matches text. Big chat machines feel alive far longer because they have seen an enormous amount of writing, but they are still matching patterns, not understanding you. Knowing that is the difference between being impressed and being fooled.
modules.challenge: Make a bot that helps someone at your local market — it asks what they want to buy and tells them the price. Get one real person to use it without you touching the phone.

words.means: a block that only runs when something is true
whatever the person types or says to the machine

modules.title: When the Machine Is Wrong
modules.bigIdea: A machine will give you a confident answer even when it has no idea — so somebody must always check.

seeThis.caption: The phone holding up a big confident percentage next to completely the wrong answer.

youNeed: your trained model from module 4, still open on the phone
the same objects
a dark corner, and a bright doorway
doThis: Show it a mango in the same light as before. It gets it right. Fine.
Now walk to a shaded corner and show the same mango. Watch the numbers wobble.
Show it a mango on a different cloth or a different floor. Note what happens.
Show it something you never trained — a shoe, a cup, a goat if one wanders past. It will still pick a box, loudly.
Write down every way you managed to break it. Three ways is good. Five is excellent.
Now retrain, this time taking photos in shade AND sun AND on two backgrounds. Test again. Better?
modules.whyItWorks: The machine only knows the world you showed it. If every training photo was taken at noon on a blue cloth, then shade is a foreign country. This is why an app trained only on tidy photos from one place can fail badly on a real farm in harmattan dust — and why the people who build good ones go and collect messy photos on purpose.
modules.challenge: Be the tester, not the builder. Take a friend's model and break it in four ways in under three minutes. Then help them fix it.

words.means: how sure the machine says it is — which can be high and still wrong
all the examples the machine learned from

modules.title: The Cardboard Sorting Machine
modules.bigIdea: Sorting done by a real machine is just a rule plus a moving part.

seeThis.caption: A cardboard chute with a flap in the middle, sending good maize one way and bad maize the other.

youNeed: a cardboard box, cut open flat
tape or thorns to pin it, a stick, string
a handful of maize grains: some fat and good, some small or broken
doThis: Cut a long strip of cardboard and fold the sides up to make a chute. Prop the top end on a stone so grain rolls down.
Halfway down, cut a hole and hinge a flap over it with tape. Tie your string to the flap.
Put a tin under the hole and a tin at the bottom of the chute. Two destinations — exactly like your two piles in module 1.
You are now the sensor. Roll grains down one at a time. Pull the string for bad grain, leave it for good grain.
Count how many you sorted in one minute. Write the number on the cardboard. That is your machine's speed.
Now let a friend pull the string while you only call out 'good' or 'bad'. Feel how the deciding and the moving became two different jobs.
modules.whyItWorks: Every real sorting machine in a grain store or a cashew factory is these two jobs joined together: something that decides (a camera and a rule) and something that moves (a flap, a puff of air, an arm). You have just built the moving half by hand and been the deciding half yourself. Bolt a camera onto your chute and you would have the whole thing.
modules.challenge: Make your chute sort three ways instead of two. Then time yourself against a friend sorting by hand — when does the machine actually win?

words.means: the part that notices something — today, your eyes
the part that moves — today, your flap

modules.title: Capstone: My Village Helper
modules.bigIdea: Pick one real problem near your home and build a machine that helps with it — then show it to someone.

seeThis.caption: A hand-drawn poster, a phone showing a trained model, and a cardboard machine, all photographed together on the ground.

youNeed: your cardboard machine from module 7
the shared phone, briefly
a big sheet of paper or flattened box, and a pen or charcoal
doThis: Choose ONE real problem you have actually seen: sorting good maize from bad, telling ripe mangoes from unripe, spotting a sick leaf.
On your poster draw three boxes in a row: what goes IN, what the machine DECIDES, what comes OUT. Big drawings, few words.
Train the phone on your two classes, using photos in sun and shade like you learned in module 6.
Set up your cardboard machine beside it. Run ten real items through, start to finish, with the phone deciding and your flap moving.
Write your score on the poster: 'Right 8 out of 10.' Be honest — an honest score is more impressive than a perfect one.
Now demonstrate it to a grown-up in under two minutes, and take one photograph of the whole setup with you beside it. That photo is your certificate.
modules.whyItWorks: You have now done every step a real engineer does: found a problem worth solving, chosen what the machine decides, trained it on your own data, tested it honestly, and explained it to someone who was not there. The cardboard is not the point. The thinking is the point, and the thinking is identical at any scale.
modules.challenge: Show your machine to someone who does this job for real — a farmer, a market trader, your grandmother. Ask them one question: 'What would make this actually useful to you?' Write their answer on the back of your poster.

words.means: a rough first build made to test an idea, not to be perfect
how many the machine got right out of how many it tried

courses.title: Make It Move
courses.tagline: If you can tell someone how to fetch water, you can program a robot.
courses.intro: Robots are not magic and they are not alive. A robot is a body that moves, a sense that notices, and a list of steps that joins the two. You are going to build all three — starting with your own legs, ending with a rover made from a jerry can and a toy motor.
courses.parentNote: Your child will learn sequencing, loops, sensing and simple mechanics without any kit at all, then apply them to a working salvaged-parts rover. By module 8 they can build a small motorised vehicle from scrap and explain how each part earns its place.

modules.title: Robot, Fetch the Water
modules.bigIdea: A robot's whole brain is a list of moves in the right order.

seeThis.caption: Footprints drawn in the dust leading in a bent path to a bucket.

youNeed: a friend to be the robot
a bucket or tin placed somewhere awkward, behind a chair or around a corner
chalk, charcoal or a stick
doThis: Draw a start box on the ground. Put your robot friend in it, facing one way. Robots never turn on their own.
You may only use four commands: FORWARD one step, TURN LEFT, TURN RIGHT, GRAB.
Say the whole list BEFORE the robot moves. Once it starts, you may not speak.
Run it. If it walks into the chair, that is not the robot's fault. Fix the list.
When it works, count your commands and write the number in the dust. Then try to beat your own number.
Hardest version: put an obstacle in the middle and get the water without touching it.
modules.whyItWorks: A real robot receives commands exactly like this — turn this wheel, move this arm, close this gripper — with no idea what a bucket is. Getting the order right, before anything moves, is the entire job. The list you shouted is what a program looks like from the inside.
modules.challenge: Blindfold your robot friend. Same task, same four commands. Suddenly your list has to be perfect, because they cannot help you.

words.means: one single instruction, like 'turn left'
commands in an order, where the order changes everything

modules.title: Why Wheels Beat Legs
modules.bigIdea: A wheel turns a hard push into an easy roll — that is why almost every robot has one.

seeThis.caption: A flat piece of cardboard with two bottle-cap wheels on a stick axle, halfway down a sloping plank.

youNeed: 4 bottle caps, a nail and a stone to punch holes
two straight sticks or old pen tubes for axles
a piece of cardboard, and a plank or board to make a slope
doThis: Punch a hole in the exact middle of each bottle cap. Off-centre holes give you a wobbly ride — try one on purpose later to see.
Push a stick through two caps to make an axle. Make two axles.
Tape the axles under your cardboard so the wheels spin freely. If they cannot spin, it is a sledge, not a cart.
Prop your plank on a stone. Race your cart down. Then drag a plain piece of cardboard down the same slope.
Watch the difference with your own eyes — the wheels win, and you can point at exactly why: the caps roll, the cardboard scrapes.
Load a small stone on top and race again. Does weight help or hurt?
modules.whyItWorks: Dragging means the whole surface fights you the entire way — that fighting is called friction. A wheel only touches the ground at one small spot at a time, and that spot rolls instead of scraping. This is why a rover crossing a field, a matatu on the road and a robot in a warehouse all use wheels, and why a bent axle ruins everything.
modules.challenge: Build a cart that rolls in a curve instead of straight. Hint: what happens if one side's wheels are bigger than the other's?

words.means: the rod a wheel spins around
the rubbing that slows things down

modules.title: Feel Before You Move
modules.bigIdea: A robot that cannot sense the world will crash into it, confidently.

seeThis.caption: A blindfolded person holding a stick out in front, just touching a wall.

youNeed: a cloth for a blindfold
a light stick or a length of stiff wire
a few obstacles: tins, stones, a chair
doThis: Lay out an obstacle course. Nothing sharp, nothing precious.
Blindfold the robot. First run: no stick, no help. Watch them creep and bump. Time it.
Second run: give them the stick. Same course. Time it again and compare the two numbers out loud.
Now write the rule they were using: 'If the stick touches something, stop and turn.' One sentence.
Swap the stick for a hand held out flat. Which sensor is better, and why? Argue it.
Last run: someone calls 'hot' and 'cold' as the robot moves. That is a different kind of sensor — which was faster?
modules.whyItWorks: That stick is a bump sensor, and real robots use exactly the same idea: a little switch on a whisker that closes when it hits something. Better robots use sound or light to feel walls before touching them, but the rule inside is always the same shape — if sensed, then act. You wrote that rule yourself.
modules.challenge: Make a course with a narrow gate. Can your stick-robot find the gap without ever touching the sides?

words.means: the part of a robot that notices something in the world
a thing in the way that the robot must not hit

modules.title: Move It On the Screen
modules.bigIdea: The same commands you shouted at your friend now make a shape move on a phone.

seeThis.caption: A phone screen with a cat sprite and three coloured blocks stacked beside it.

youNeed: one shared phone with a browser and a block-coding site (Scratch works in a phone browser; turn it sideways)
patience with small fingers on a small screen
your command list from module 1, written down
doThis: Turn the phone sideways. Everything is easier sideways.
Drag one 'move 10 steps' block under the green flag and tap it. The cat shifts. That tiny movement is your first program running.
Add 'turn 90 degrees'. Then another move. You are writing exactly the list you shouted in module 1.
Draw a square path. Four moves, four turns. If your square comes out crooked, check your turn number.
Now recreate your module 1 water route on the screen, obstacle and all. Draw the bucket as a second sprite.
Tap the green flag and watch your dust-path from week one run inside a phone.
modules.whyItWorks: Nothing new happened here — that is the lesson. Blocks are just your spoken commands written in a way a machine can obey. This is why doing it with your body first was not a waste of time: you already knew the hard part before you touched the screen.
modules.challenge: Program a triangle without being told the turn number. Get it wrong, look at the shape, and adjust. That is how real engineers find numbers.

words.means: a character or shape on the screen you can move
your list of commands, written for a machine

modules.title: The Phone Is Full of Sensors
modules.bigIdea: That shared phone already has more sensors than most robots — you just have to look.

seeThis.caption: A phone tilted at an angle with a compass needle swinging on the screen.

youNeed: the shared phone
a free compass or sensor-reading app, or the built-in compass
a nail or a small magnet if you can find one
doThis: Open the compass. Turn slowly in a circle and watch the number change. The phone feels the Earth's magnetic field — that is a sensor.
Bring a nail or magnet close. Watch the number go mad, then take it away. You just jammed a sensor.
Tilt the phone slowly and watch the screen rotate. Something inside is feeling which way is down.
Cover the little sensor near the top of the screen with your thumb during a call. The screen goes black — point at it. That is a proximity sensor doing exactly what your stick did in module 3.
Write a list: every sensor you found in ten minutes. Aim for four.
For each one, write one job a robot could do with it. Example: compass, so a rover always heads back to the borehole.
modules.whyItWorks: Sensors turn something in the world — tilt, direction, light, nearness — into a number a machine can use in a rule. A drone stays level with the same kind of tilt sensor you just found in a phone. Once you see sensors as number-makers, robots stop being mysterious.
modules.challenge: Design a robot on paper that uses THREE of the sensors you found. Draw it and label what each sensor is for.

words.means: the invisible pull that makes a compass point north
how near something is

modules.title: Loops Save Your Legs
modules.bigIdea: Say it once, wrap it in a loop, and the machine repeats it forever without getting bored.

seeThis.caption: One pair of blocks inside a big curved arrow marked with the number four.

youNeed: the shared phone with your block project from module 4
a friend to be a human loop
somewhere to walk in a square
doThis: First with bodies: instead of shouting eight commands for a square, shout 'repeat four times: forward, turn right'. Watch your friend do it.
On the phone, find the 'repeat' block. Drag your move-and-turn pair inside it. Set it to 4.
Run it. Same square, half the blocks. Count the blocks you deleted — that number is what a loop saved you.
Change 4 to 3 and the turn to 120. Watch a triangle appear. One number, whole new shape.
Put a 'forever' loop around everything and add a small turn. Watch it spin until you stop it.
Now try to draw a circle. Big repeat number, tiny turn. Point at the moment it stops looking like a polygon.
modules.whyItWorks: Loops are why robots can do the boring jobs. A machine sorting maize does not need a million instructions — it needs one instruction wrapped in 'do this again'. And a robot's main brain loop, running hundreds of times a second, is exactly this: check the sensors, decide, move, repeat.
modules.challenge: Draw a five-pointed star using only one repeat block. You will need to work out the turn number by trying — that is allowed and expected.

words.means: an instruction to do something again and again
the block that says how many times

modules.title: The Jerry-Can Rover
modules.bigIdea: A dead toy still has a live motor inside it, and that motor can carry your robot.

seeThis.caption: Half a plastic jerry can on bottle-cap wheels, with a small motor taped to the back and wires running to a battery.

youNeed: a small DC motor from a broken toy car, fan or CD player
a battery holder or two AA cells, plus wire or foil strips
a cut-open jerry can or strong plastic bottle, caps for wheels, tape, and an adult nearby for cutting
doThis: SAFETY FIRST: only small batteries — AA or AAA. Never mains electricity, never a car battery, never a charging cable cut open. Ask an adult to do the cutting.
Touch the motor's two wires to the two ends of the battery. It spins. Now swap the wires over. It spins backwards — point at that. You just learned how a robot reverses.
Cut the jerry can into a low open boat shape. That is your chassis. Fit your bottle-cap axles from module 2 underneath.
Tape the motor at the back so its shaft touches one wheel, or push a cap onto the shaft to make a drive wheel. This takes fiddling. Fiddling is the job.
Twist a wire loose so the rover stops, twist it back so it goes. That loose wire is your switch.
Let it run across the yard. It will veer. Measure how far it goes before it leaves a straight line — write the number on the can.
modules.whyItWorks: You now have all three robot parts in one object: a body (the can), an actuator (the motor), and a control (your wire switch). Swapping the wires reverses the motor because you reversed the direction of the current — real robots do that with a little circuit instead of your fingers, but the trick is identical. It veers because no two wheels ever grip quite the same, which is why real rovers constantly correct themselves.
modules.challenge: Make it go straighter without buying anything. Try heavier at the front, wider wheels, or a small trailing stick at the back. Measure before and after.

words.means: the part that turns electricity into spinning
the body frame everything else is attached to
the complete loop electricity travels around

modules.title: Capstone: The Carrier Rover
modules.bigIdea: Give your rover one real job to do, prove it works, and photograph the proof.

seeThis.caption: The jerry-can rover carrying a small load of maize cobs across a chalk line, with a hand holding a phone taking the picture.

youNeed: your rover from module 7
a load to carry: maize cobs, stones, a small tin of water
chalk or a stick to mark a course, and the shared phone for one photo
doThis: Mark a start line and a finish line about five big steps apart. Mark them properly — a real test needs a real course.
Run 1: empty rover. Time it and write the time on the jerry can.
Now load it. Add weight until it stops moving, then take one item off. That is your rover's maximum load — find the real number, do not guess.
Improve ONE thing: bigger wheels, motor mounted tighter, load moved forward. Change one thing only, or you will never know what helped.
Run the loaded course three times. Write all three times down, including the bad one. Three honest numbers beat one lucky number.
Take one photograph: rover, load, course and you. Then explain to somebody, in under a minute, what each part does and what you would fix next.
modules.whyItWorks: You just ran a proper engineering test: a fixed course, a baseline measurement, one change at a time, and repeated runs. That method is the same whether you are testing a cardboard rover or a machine that hauls sacks in a warehouse. And your list of what you would fix next is the most valuable thing you made today.
modules.challenge: Race a friend's rover — but score it on load carried, not speed. The slow strong one usually wins, and that surprises everyone.

words.means: the load a machine is built to carry
a fair try, repeated, with the numbers written down

courses.title: Eyes in the Sky
courses.tagline: A drone is not a toy that flies. It is a camera that can stand on air.
courses.intro: Look up. Everything a drone does — push air down, hold itself steady, look at the ground from above — you can understand with paper, string and a bit of running about. You will also learn the rules of the sky, because the sky belongs to everybody and it has real laws.
courses.parentNote: Your child will understand lift, propellers, aerial mapping and — importantly — the genuine safety and legal rules around flying, all without owning a drone. The final project is a real overhead photo map of a place they know, made from a pole and a phone.

modules.title: Push the Air Down
modules.bigIdea: Nothing flies by wanting to. Things fly by pushing air downwards, hard.

seeThis.caption: A sheet of paper held flat and swung down fast, with the hand feeling the push back upwards.

youNeed: two sheets of paper or thin cardboard, one flat and one crumpled into a ball
a plastic bag
a bit of open space
doThis: Hold the flat sheet and the crumpled ball high, one in each hand. Drop them together. Watch which lands first.
Say why out loud: the flat one has to shove a lot of air out of the way, so the air holds it up longer.
Now hold a sheet flat in your hand and swing it down fast. Feel the push back against your palm. That push is lift, and you can feel it right now.
Open the plastic bag, hold it by the handles and run. It fills and drags behind you. That drag is the same air fighting back.
Wave a piece of cardboard downwards over a pile of dust. The dust flies away from you. Point at it — that is the air being pushed down.
Last: drop the flat sheet edge-on instead of flat. It falls fast. Same paper, different amount of air pushed.
modules.whyItWorks: A drone hovers by throwing air downwards all the time. The air pushes back with the same strength, and that push holds the drone up. If it pushes a bit harder, it rises; a bit softer, it sinks. Everything else on a drone is just clever ways of controlling how hard each propeller pushes.
modules.challenge: Make a paper shape that takes longest to reach the ground from the same height. Test three designs and time each one.

words.means: the upward push that holds a flying thing up
the air pushing back against something moving through it

modules.title: Four Spinning Hands
modules.bigIdea: A propeller is a slanted blade that turns spinning into pushing.

seeThis.caption: A paper spinner twirling down through the air, next to four hands spread out in a square.

youNeed: paper and scissors
a paperclip, small stone or bit of clay for weight
somewhere high but safe to drop from, like standing on a step
doThis: Cut a strip of paper. Cut a slit down the middle at the top and fold the two flaps in opposite directions. Clip a weight at the bottom.
Drop it from as high as you can safely reach. It spins as it falls — point at the spin. Bent blades turn falling into turning.
Now bend both flaps the SAME way and drop it. It flutters and drops. The slant is what makes the spin.
Make a second spinner with the flaps bent the other way. Drop both together and watch them spin in opposite directions.
Hold your two spinners side by side, then imagine two more. That square of four is exactly how a quadcopter is built.
Blow steadily on one flap and watch the whole thing turn. Air on a slanted blade always becomes turning — or the other way round, turning becomes moving air.
modules.whyItWorks: A drone propeller is that same slanted blade, just driven by a motor instead of by falling. As it spins it scoops air and flings it downwards, and the air pushes the drone up. A quadcopter has four of them so it can push harder on one side than the other and lean where it wants to go.
modules.challenge: Change one thing — longer blades, heavier weight, wider flaps — and see if you can double how many spins it makes on the way down. Count them.

words.means: a spinning slanted blade that pushes air
a flying machine with four propellers

modules.title: The World From a Bird's Eye
modules.bigIdea: Seen from straight above, a place you know turns into a map.

seeThis.caption: A compound drawn in chalk as seen from above: square for the house, blobs for trees, a line for the path.

youNeed: chalk, charcoal or a stick, and a flat patch of ground
stones and leaves as markers
somewhere higher to stand: a step, a wall, a low branch with an adult watching
doThis: Stand somewhere a bit higher and look down at your compound or school yard. Not out — DOWN.
Notice what shape each thing is from above. A house is a rectangle. A tree is a circle. A path is a line. A goat is a small moving blob.
On the ground, draw the whole place as if you were the bird. Start with the biggest thing and work down.
Put a stone on your map where you are standing right now. Have a friend walk to a spot, and point to where they are on your map.
Add a north arrow using the sun: sunrise side is east. Every real map has one.
Now walk your route to the water point in real life, then draw that same route on your map as a dotted line.
modules.whyItWorks: This is exactly what a drone gives people: the straight-down view that turns a confusing place into a clear map. It is how a farmer counts how many trees are in a field, how people work out where a flood is spreading, and how someone plans a new road. The hard skill is not flying — it is reading what you see.
modules.challenge: Draw your map from memory, then go and check it. Mark every mistake in a different colour. Mistakes found are points scored.

words.means: the view looking straight down from above
a drawing of a place from above, with things in the right positions

modules.title: Fly It Inside the Phone
modules.bigIdea: Learning to fly is learning to keep track of which way the drone is facing.

seeThis.caption: A phone held sideways showing a small aircraft hovering above a field, with two thumb circles on the screen.

youNeed: one shared phone with a browser and a free flight simulator page, or a free simulator app
a flat surface to rest the phone on
ten quiet minutes
doThis: Open the simulator and just hover. Do not try to fly anywhere yet. Getting it to stay still is lesson one.
Practise up and down only. Notice you are always making small corrections — it never just sits there by itself.
Now fly it away from you and turn left. Easy. Now fly it back TOWARDS you and turn left. Your controls feel backwards — this catches everybody.
Say the reason out loud: left is the drone's left, not yours. When it faces you, its left is your right.
Draw a square in the air, flying forward and turning at each corner, keeping the nose always pointing the way you travel.
Crash it on purpose once. In a simulator, that is free. That is the entire reason simulators exist.
modules.whyItWorks: Everybody's first real crash is the same one: the drone turns around, the controls feel reversed, and panic does the rest. Practising that in a simulator costs nothing and saves a real machine that is worth more than a term's school fees. Professional pilots keep using simulators for exactly this reason.
modules.challenge: Fly a figure of eight without letting the nose swing wildly. Then do it again with the drone facing you the whole time.

words.means: to stay still in the air in one spot
a pretend version on a screen where crashing is free

modules.title: The Sky Has Rules
modules.bigIdea: The sky is shared, so flying is not just about skill — it is about law and other people's safety.

seeThis.caption: A red no-entry sign between a small drone and a big aeroplane, and another between a drone and someone's house.

youNeed: the shared phone to look up your own country's rules
paper to write your own pilot's pledge
a grown-up to talk it through with
doThis: Learn the big one first: never fly near an airport or where aeroplanes take off and land. This is banned almost everywhere, and it is dangerous, not just naughty.

Learn the second: in many African countries — Kenya, Nigeria, Ghana, Rwanda, South Africa and others — drones must be registered and you need permission before flying. Rules differ by country, so you must check YOUR country's civil aviation authority.
Search on the phone for your own country's civil aviation authority drone rules. Write down two real rules you find.
Now the people rules: do not fly over crowds, do not fly over someone's home or compound without asking, keep the drone where you can see it.
Ask yourself the question that matters: 'How would I feel if a stranger's camera hovered over my yard?' Write your answer down.
Write and sign your own Pilot's Pledge: five rules in your own words. Stick it somewhere you will see it.
modules.whyItWorks: Drones are genuinely useful in Africa — carrying blood and medicine to clinics, counting cattle, checking crops and finding people after floods — and all of that depends on pilots being trusted. One careless flight near an airport or over a private compound damages that trust for everybody. Rules are what keep a good tool from being banned.
modules.challenge: Find out one real, useful job drones do in your own country and one thing that is banned. Tell someone both facts.

words.means: the sky above a place, and who is allowed to use it
officially recording a drone with the authorities, which many countries require
a person's right not to be watched or filmed without permission

modules.title: Camera Eyes
modules.bigIdea: Many overlapping photos from above can be joined into one big picture of a whole place.

seeThis.caption: Three photos of the ground overlapping at the edges, lined up to make one long strip.

youNeed: the shared phone camera
a long stick, a broom handle or a safe raised spot
tape, and a flat area to photograph such as a yard or garden bed
doThis: Hold the phone as high as you safely can, pointing straight down. Take one photo.
Take three steps sideways and take another — but make sure about a third of the first photo is still in this one. That overlap is the whole trick.
Keep going in a straight line for five or six photos, always with the same height and the same overlap.
Look at them side by side on the screen. Find the same stone or leaf appearing in two photos — point at it. That shared thing is how photos get joined.
Print or sketch them and lay them out overlapping to make one long picture of the ground.
Now do it again from lower down. Notice you see more detail but need far more photos to cover the same ground.
modules.whyItWorks: A drone mapping a field flies straight lines like a person ploughing, taking photos with a big overlap. Software finds the same points in overlapping photos and stitches them into one huge map. Fly low and you get fine detail but a slow job; fly high and you cover ground fast but see less. Every mapping pilot chooses between those two, every single flight.
modules.challenge: Map something small and messy from above — a rubbish patch, a vegetable bed, a goat pen — with six photos. Can someone else recognise the place from your strip alone?

words.means: the part of the ground that shows up in two photos
joining many photos into one big picture

modules.title: Make Your Own Thrust
modules.bigIdea: Thrust is a force you can actually measure, not a word from a book.

seeThis.caption: A motor with a paper propeller on one end of a balanced stick, with stones piled on the other end.

youNeed: a small DC motor from a broken toy or fan, plus AA batteries and wire
stiff paper or a plastic bottle to cut a small propeller, and a small cap to fix it to the shaft
a straight stick, a stone to balance it on, string, and small stones as weights — with an adult supervising
doThis: SAFETY: spinning blades hurt. Keep fingers, faces and little brothers away. Use paper or thin plastic blades only, never metal. Wear something over your eyes if you can, and never lean over it.
Cut a small two-bladed propeller and twist each blade the same amount in opposite directions — like your paper spinner in module 2. Fix it to the motor shaft.
Balance your stick across a stone like a see-saw. Tape the motor at one end, pointing so it blows DOWNWARDS.
Run the motor. Watch that end of the stick lift. That lift is thrust and you are looking straight at it.
Now add small stones to the other end until the stick balances level. Those stones weigh the same as your thrust — you have just measured a force.
Change one thing: flatter blades, more twist, or a fresh battery. Measure again in stones. Write both numbers down side by side.
modules.whyItWorks: Drone engineers do exactly this on a proper test stand, using grams instead of stones, because a drone can only fly if its total thrust beats its total weight. That is why every extra gram — a bigger battery, a heavier camera — costs flying time. You have now measured the same trade-off with a stick and a pile of stones.
modules.challenge: Find the blade twist that gives the most thrust. Test three different twists, record the stones for each, and be honest if your favourite design loses.

words.means: the push a propeller makes
a push or pull you can measure

modules.title: Capstone: My Place From Above
modules.bigIdea: Make a real overhead map of somewhere you know, and tell people something they did not know about it.

seeThis.caption: A stitched photo strip taped onto card, with hand-drawn labels and arrows pointing at things, photographed flat on the ground.

youNeed: the shared phone, a long stick or safe high spot
card or flattened box, tape, and a pen
your Pilot's Pledge from module 5
doThis: Pick your place: your compound, the school yard, a garden plot, the space around a borehole or water tap.
Plan first. Draw on paper the straight lines you will walk and where each photo goes, with a third overlap. A plan makes a map; wandering makes a mess.
Take your photos, high and pointing straight down, walking your planned lines. Do not change height halfway.
Lay them out overlapping on the card and tape them into one picture. Add a title, a north arrow and a scale note like 'this path is about 20 of my steps long'.
Now find something interesting IN the map that you cannot see from the ground: where water collects, where a path is worn, where there is empty space that could be planted. Label it with an arrow.
Copy your Pilot's Pledge onto the back. Then photograph the finished map with your hand in the picture, and show it to someone who uses that place every day.
modules.whyItWorks: You have done the actual work of aerial mapping: plan the lines, keep a steady height, hold your overlap, stitch, label and — most importantly — find the one thing in the picture worth telling someone. Real drone surveys live or die on that last step. The flying is the easy part; noticing is the skill.
modules.challenge: Map the same place at two different times — morning and evening, or dry day and after rain. Put the two maps side by side and mark every difference you can find.

words.means: carefully looking at and recording a place
how big something on the map is compared to real life

courses.title: AI: Build & Break It
courses.tagline: Anyone can train a model. You are going to learn where it fails — and that is the valuable part.
courses.intro: You will build classifiers, then attack them until they fall over. Not because breaking things is fun — though it is — but because the person who knows exactly where a system fails is the person worth hiring. We start on the ground with beans and chalk, because the maths is easier to see than to read.
courses.parentNote: Your teenager will move from hands-on intuition for features and decision boundaries to training and honestly evaluating a real image classifier, including precision, recall and dataset bias. By module 8 they can write a simple classifier in Python on a phone and document its limitations like a professional.

modules.title: Features, Not Magic
modules.bigIdea: A machine never sees a mango — it sees a short list of numbers you chose to measure.

seeThis.caption: A single bean beside a handwritten row of three numbers: length, width, spots.

youNeed: about 30 beans, maize grains or groundnuts, ideally a mix of good and damaged
a strip of paper marked in finger-widths as a ruler
paper and pen, or chalk and a flat stone
doThis: Pick one grain. Write down three numbers about it: length, width, and number of dark marks. That row of numbers is called a feature vector.
Do this for 20 grains. Mark each row G for good or D for damaged. You now have a dataset — a real one, that you made.
Draw two axes on the ground: length across, width up. Plot every grain as a dot, writing G or D beside it.
Stand back and look. Do the G dots cluster away from the D dots? If they do, your features are useful. If they are all mixed together, they are not.
Now throw away width and try 'number of dark marks' instead. Re-plot. Which pair of features separates them better? Point at the better picture.
Write one sentence: 'The feature that separates good from damaged best is ___.' That sentence is the whole of feature selection.
modules.whyItWorks: Every image classifier begins by turning a picture into numbers. Modern networks learn which numbers to extract instead of being told, but the principle you just used is unchanged: if your chosen features do not separate the classes, no amount of clever maths afterwards will save you. Choosing what to measure is the highest-leverage decision in the whole pipeline.
modules.challenge: Find a pair of features where the two groups overlap almost completely. Then explain why that pair is useless, using your own plot as evidence.

words.means: one measurable property of a thing, expressed as a number
the full list of numbers describing one example
a collection of examples, each with its features and its true label

modules.title: Be the Classifier
modules.bigIdea: Classifying is drawing a line through your data and deciding which side new things fall on.

seeThis.caption: A chalk grid on the ground with two clusters of stones separated by a straight chalk line, and one unknown stone sitting near it.

youNeed: your plotted data from module 1, or chalk to redraw it
stones in two colours, or stones and bottle caps
a long straight stick or string
doThis: Redraw your two axes big, on the ground. Place a stone for every good grain and a cap for every damaged one, at its measured position.
Lay your stick down as a straight line that best separates stones from caps. Move it until you cannot do better.
Count the mistakes: stones on the wrong side, caps on the wrong side. Write that number down. A perfect split is rare and slightly suspicious.
Take a NEW grain, measure it, place it. Which side of the stick? That is your prediction. Now check the real answer.
Second method: for that same new grain, find its three nearest neighbours on the ground and take a vote. Did the two methods agree?
Now curve your line using string instead of a stick. Can you get zero mistakes? And do you trust a line that twists around every single dot?
modules.whyItWorks: You have just built two real classifiers by hand. The straight stick is a linear classifier; the vote of nearest points is k-nearest-neighbours, still used in production today. And the twisting string is overfitting: a boundary so contorted to fit your exact examples that it will do badly on the next grain it meets. That tension between fitting your data and generalising to new data is the central problem in machine learning.
modules.challenge: Split your data in half. Fit your line using only the first half, then test it on the second half you never looked at. Report both error counts. That gap is what the field really cares about.

words.means: a system that assigns a new example to one of several classes
the line or surface separating one class's region from another's
matching your training examples so exactly that you fail on new ones

modules.title: Garbage In, Garbage Out
modules.bigIdea: A model can only be as fair and as accurate as the data you collected — and collecting is a choice.

seeThis.caption: Five samples pulled from the same easy-to-reach heap, and one lonely sample from everywhere else.

youNeed: access to a real pile of something varied — grain, mangoes, stones, leaves
paper for tallies
a friend to sample separately from you
doThis: Grab 20 items from the pile without thinking. Tally how many are good and how many are damaged. That is your quick sample.
Now dig properly: take items from the bottom, the edges, the middle, the bit hidden behind. Another 20. Tally again.
Compare the two tallies. They will differ. Say out loud why: the easy grab took what was on top, and what is on top is not random.
Write down three real ways a dataset could get skewed: only photos taken in bright sun, only from one farm, only of the crop somebody already suspected was sick.
Now the serious one. Imagine an app trained only on tidy photos from one region, then used across a whole country. Write down who gets a wrong answer and what it costs them.
Design a fair sampling plan for your pile in five written steps. Then follow it and see whether your tally changes again.
modules.whyItWorks: Sampling bias is not a rare accident, it is the default outcome of convenient data collection. A crop-disease model trained on well-lit photos of one variety from one area can drop sharply in accuracy on a different soil, a different variety, or in harmattan dust. The fix is boring and unglamorous: go and deliberately collect the awkward cases nobody else bothered with.
modules.challenge: Deliberately build a biased dataset that scores brilliantly on its own test and would fail badly in reality. Then explain the trick to someone — and notice how convincing your fake score looked.

words.means: when the examples you collected do not represent the real world
a sample that reflects the true variety of what you will meet
to work well on new data you have never seen

modules.title: Train a Real Classifier
modules.bigIdea: With a shared phone and forty photos you can train a working image classifier in ten minutes.

seeThis.caption: A phone screen with two labelled photo sets — healthy leaves and marked leaves — and a confidence bar.

youNeed: one shared phone with a browser and internet for about 20 minutes
two visibly different classes of real things: healthy vs blemished cassava or maize leaves, ripe vs unripe mangoes
daylight and a plain background such as a cloth or bare ground
doThis: Open a free in-browser training tool (Google's Teachable Machine runs in a phone browser and needs no account).
Create Class A and capture around 40 images, rotating and re-angling the object as you go. Variety inside a class is what makes it robust.
Create Class B the same way. Deliberately include some awkward examples — half-shade, slightly blurred, held differently.
Train. Then test on items the model has never seen and record the confidence numbers for ten of them in a table.
Note something important: the two confidence numbers always add to 100%. The model cannot say 'I don't know' — it can only divide certainty between the boxes you gave it.
Add a third class called 'nothing' — bare ground, hands, random objects — and retrain. Test again. Did the false alarms drop?
modules.whyItWorks: That third class is a genuine professional technique. A two-class model forced to choose will confidently mislabel anything unfamiliar, which is how a leaf-disease app ends up diagnosing a shoe. Giving it a background or 'none of these' class gives it somewhere honest to put the unknown. Real deployed systems also set a confidence threshold below which they refuse to answer at all.
modules.challenge: Build the same classifier twice: once with 20 images per class, once with 60. Test both on the identical ten items and report the difference in a table. Does more data always win?

words.means: one of the categories a classifier can output
the model's score for each class, which is not the same as being right
the confidence level below which you refuse to trust the answer

modules.title: Break Your Own Model
modules.bigIdea: You do not understand a system until you can make it fail on demand.

seeThis.caption: The same leaf, now dusty and in low light, getting a confident and completely wrong answer.

youNeed: your trained model from module 4
the same objects plus some deliberately awkward ones
a notebook for your attack log, and varied light: shade, doorway, evening
doThis: Start an attack log with three columns: what I changed, what it predicted, confidence.
Attack 1 — lighting. Test in shade, in direct sun, near a doorway, at dusk. Log every result.
Attack 2 — background. Same object on cloth, on red laterite soil, on a wooden bench, in a hand. Log it.
Attack 3 — occlusion and dust. Cover part of the object, or dust it lightly. Log the confidence, especially when it stays high while being wrong.
Attack 4 — out of distribution. Show it something from neither class. Note how loudly it commits to a wrong answer.
Now rank your attacks by damage done, and write the single sentence a user of this app would most need to be warned about.
modules.whyItWorks: This is red-teaming, and it is a paid job. High confidence on a wrong answer is the most dangerous failure mode there is, because it defeats the human check. Systems that make real decisions — approving a loan, flagging a diseased field, identifying a person — are tested exactly this way before anyone is allowed to rely on them.
modules.challenge: Swap models with a friend. You get five minutes to break theirs, they get five to break yours. Then each of you fixes the top failure the other found and re-tests.

words.means: how well a model holds up when conditions change
input unlike anything the model was trained on
a specific, repeatable way a system goes wrong

modules.title: The Confusion Matrix
modules.bigIdea: One accuracy number hides everything that matters — you need to know which mistakes it makes.

seeThis.caption: A hand-drawn two-by-two grid of tallies: correct answers on the diagonal, mistakes off it.

youNeed: your model and at least 20 test items with known true labels
paper and pen for the grid
the attack log from module 5
doThis: Draw a 2x2 grid. Rows are the truth, columns are the prediction. Label them clearly before you start.
Test 20 items and put a tally mark in the correct cell each time. No skipping the embarrassing ones.
Count the diagonal — those are your correct answers. Divide by 20 for accuracy.
Now look at the two off-diagonal cells. One is a false alarm (healthy called diseased); the other is a miss (diseased called healthy). Write which is which.
Ask the question that matters: which mistake is worse HERE? A false alarm wastes a farmer's spray. A miss lets disease spread through the field. Decide, and justify it in one sentence.

Now imagine a lazy model that says 'healthy' every time on a pile where only 1 in 10 is diseased. Work out its accuracy. It scores 90% and is completely useless — that is why accuracy alone is a trap.
modules.whyItWorks: The confusion matrix separates two errors that a single accuracy figure blends together, and they almost never cost the same. In medical screening a miss is far worse than a false alarm; in a spam filter it is the reverse. Precision and recall are just two ways of reading this grid, and choosing which one to optimise is a decision about consequences, not about maths.
modules.challenge: Deliberately shift your model to make almost no misses, and observe the false alarms shoot up. Draw both matrices side by side and explain the trade to someone who has never heard of it.

words.means: the model says yes when the truth is no
the model says no when the truth is yes
of all the real cases, the fraction the model actually caught

modules.title: Write the Classifier in Python
modules.bigIdea: The algorithm you did with stones on the ground is about fifteen lines of Python.

seeThis.caption: A phone screen with a short Python function and a printed prediction beneath it.

youNeed: the shared phone with a Python app that runs offline (Pydroid 3 or similar) or an online editor
your measured dataset from module 1, on paper
patience: typing code on a phone is slow, so type carefully rather than fast
doThis: Type your dataset in as a list of rows, each row being [length, width, label]. Print it. Seeing your own paper data appear on screen is the moment it becomes real.
Write a distance function: for two feature vectors, add up the squared differences and return that. Six lines at most.
Write classify(new_item): compute the distance to every stored example, find the smallest, and return that example's label. This is 1-nearest-neighbour, complete.
Test it on an item you know the answer to. When it prints the right label, you have written a working classifier from scratch with no libraries at all.
Upgrade to k=3: sort the distances, take the three closest, return the majority label. Compare k=1 and k=3 on the same test items.
Finally, loop over ten test items and print an accuracy score. Take a screenshot of the output — that is your evidence.
modules.whyItWorks: k-nearest-neighbours has no training step at all: it simply remembers everything and compares. That makes it slow at prediction time and hungry for memory, which is precisely why other algorithms exist. Having written one yourself, you now know that machine learning is not sorcery — it is arithmetic, arranged carefully, on features you chose.
modules.challenge: Add a third feature to every row and see whether accuracy improves. Then remove your best feature and watch it collapse. Both experiments teach more than reading about them.

words.means: predict by finding the k most similar stored examples and taking a vote
a number saying how unalike two feature vectors are
a named block of code you can call again with different inputs

modules.title: Capstone: A Classifier That Serves Someone
modules.bigIdea: Build a classifier for one real person's real problem, test it honestly, and publish its limits alongside its results.

seeThis.caption: A one-page report on a board: the problem, the confusion matrix, the failure list, and a warning box — photographed with the phone beside it.

youNeed: the shared phone, your trained model, and your Python code
one real person willing to describe a problem they actually have
paper or card for a one-page report
doThis: Interview one real person — a farmer, a trader, a shopkeeper, a nurse — and write down one classification they make by eye every day. Their words, not yours.
Collect your own dataset for it, deliberately including awkward conditions: shade, dust, different backgrounds. Aim for 60 images across your classes plus a 'none of these' class.
Train the model, then split off ten items it has never seen and build a confusion matrix from them. Report the real numbers, including the bad ones.
Run your module 5 attacks and write a LIMITATIONS section: at least four specific conditions under which this model should not be trusted.
State a threshold rule in one sentence, such as: 'Below 80% confidence, this tool must not be used to decide anything — ask a person.'

Lay out your one-page report: the problem in the person's own words, how it works, the matrix, the limitations, the threshold. Photograph it. Then show it back to the person you interviewed and write down what they say.
modules.whyItWorks: The limitations section is the part that separates a school project from professional work. Anyone can post an accuracy number; stating precisely where your system must not be trusted is what makes it safe to use, and it is exactly what a model card in industry contains. You have now built, tested, attacked, bounded and documented a machine learning system end to end.
modules.challenge: Give your report to someone who has never met you and ask them: 'Would you rely on this, and why not?' Their objection is your next project.

words.means: a short document stating what a model does, how well, and where it fails
putting a model to work on real decisions with real consequences
a stated condition under which your system should not be trusted

courses.title: Robotics with Python
courses.tagline: Sense, think, act — a hundred times a second. That loop is every robot ever built.
courses.intro: You will learn control the way engineers actually think about it: as a loop that reads the world, decides, and moves — then does it again immediately. We start in the sand because a control loop is much easier to understand when you have walked one, and we finish with a servo arm you built from salvage and drive with your own Python.
courses.parentNote: Your teenager will learn control loops, state machines, PWM and proportional control conceptually first, then implement them in Python on a shared phone and finally on salvaged hardware. By module 8 they can build and program a working servo-driven sorting arm and explain the control logic behind it.

modules.title: The Loop, Drawn in Sand
modules.bigIdea: Every robot on Earth runs the same three-step loop, forever: sense, decide, act.

seeThis.caption: Three circles drawn in the sand joined by arrows into a ring, with a stick balanced on a fingertip beside them.

youNeed: a long stick or broom handle
sand, dust or chalk to draw on
a friend and something to time with
doThis: Balance the stick upright on your open palm. Keep it up for thirty seconds. You will be moving constantly.
Now freeze your hand completely and try again. It falls almost immediately. Say why: with no correcting, there is no control.
Draw the loop in the sand: SENSE (eyes see it tilting), DECIDE (which way and how much), ACT (move hand), then an arrow back to SENSE.
Balance it again but blink hard and often. Note how much worse it gets. You have just reduced your sensor's update rate.
Now try with your arm moving in slow motion on purpose. It falls. That is actuator lag, and it kills control loops.
Time three runs: normal, blinking, slow-motion. Write the three numbers down — that table is a real experiment about loop rate and lag.
modules.whyItWorks: A drone holding position, a self-balancing scooter and a line-following robot all run this loop hundreds or thousands of times a second. Your experiments showed the two things that break it: sensing too rarely, and acting too slowly. Every serious control engineering decision comes back to those two numbers.
modules.challenge: Balance the stick while a friend gently nudges it at random. Then describe, in three sentences, how your loop changed to cope with a disturbance.

words.means: the repeating cycle of sensing, deciding and acting
using the result of your last action to choose the next one
the delay between sensing something and acting on it

modules.title: State Machines with Bottle Caps
modules.bigIdea: A machine is always in exactly one state, and only certain events can move it to another.

seeThis.caption: Three bottle caps laid on the ground with chalk arrows between them, each arrow labelled with what causes the move.

youNeed: four or five bottle caps and chalk
a real system to model: a borehole pump, a traffic light, a mobile-money transaction
paper for your final diagram
doThis: Choose a borehole pump controller. List its states on separate caps: IDLE, PUMPING, TANK FULL, FAULT.
Lay the caps out with space between them and draw an arrow for every legal move. Label each arrow with its trigger: 'button pressed', 'float switch high', 'motor too hot'.
Now find an illegal move. Can you go from IDLE straight to TANK FULL? No. Cross that arrow out — the arrows you refuse to draw are what makes the machine safe.
Play it: a friend calls out events at random and you physically move a stone from cap to cap. Any event with no arrow is simply ignored.
Add the awkward one: what happens if power fails mid-pump and comes back? Which state should it wake in? Argue it, then decide and draw it.
Copy the finished diagram onto paper. That drawing is a genuine engineering document and it is what you would code from.
modules.whyItWorks: State machines are how real controllers stay predictable, from washing machines to lift doors to mobile-money flows. The value is not the states, it is the transitions you deliberately do not allow — that is how you guarantee a pump cannot run dry or a lift cannot open between floors. Load-shedding makes the power-fail transition a genuinely important design question here, not a hypothetical one.
modules.challenge: Model something with at least six states — a matatu fare collection, a maize mill, a phone charging from a solar panel. Find one transition everybody forgets, then add it.

words.means: one distinct situation the system can be in at a moment
a permitted move from one state to another
the thing that happens and triggers a transition

modules.title: Human PWM
modules.bigIdea: You can make a switch that is only ever fully on or fully off behave like a dial — by flicking it fast.

seeThis.caption: Two rows of blocks and gaps drawn in chalk, one half filled, one nearly solid.

youNeed: a torch, phone light or candle and a hand to block it
someone to keep a steady beat by clapping
chalk and paper
doThis: Beat time steadily, one beat per second. Turn the torch on for one beat, off for one beat, repeatedly. That is 50 percent duty cycle.
Now do on-on-on-off. That is 75 percent. Draw both patterns as filled and empty boxes on the ground.
Speed up until you are flicking several times per second. Look at the light out of the corner of your eye — it starts to look dim rather than flashing.
Try 25 percent fast. It looks dimmer still. You are controlling brightness with a switch that has no dimmer at all.
Write the formula yourself: average power equals duty cycle times full power. Check it against what you saw.
Last: flick slowly on purpose. The flicker returns. That is why PWM frequency matters as much as duty cycle.
modules.whyItWorks: This is pulse width modulation, and it is how nearly every motor speed and LED brightness is controlled in real electronics. Transistors are efficient when fully on or fully off and waste energy in between, so instead of throttling the current you switch it rapidly and vary the on-time. A motor's own inertia smooths the pulses the same way your eye smoothed the torch.
modules.challenge: Two of you flick torches at different duty cycles at the same speed. Can a third person rank them by brightness without being told the numbers? Test whether people can tell 60 from 70.

words.means: pulse width modulation: switching fast and varying the on-time to control power
the percentage of each cycle the switch spends on
how many complete on-off cycles happen per second

modules.title: Python in the Browser
modules.bigIdea: Variables, loops and functions are the only three things you need before you can control anything.

seeThis.caption: A phone in landscape showing four lines of Python and the printed output beneath.

youNeed: the shared phone with a browser Python editor, or an offline Python app such as Pydroid 3
phone in landscape and, if possible, a keyboard app with a number row
paper to write code out before typing it
doThis: Write code on paper first. Typing on a phone is slow, so make the slow part count — this habit alone will save you hours.
Type: speed = 50, then print(speed). Change it to 80 and print again. A variable is a labelled box you can change.
Write a loop that prints the numbers 1 to 4. Then wrap your square-driving commands in it, printing 'forward' and 'turn' each time.
Write a function drive_square(steps) that takes a number and prints the right instructions. Call it twice with different numbers.
Add an if statement: if battery < 20, print 'RETURN HOME'. Set battery to different values and watch which branch runs.
Now combine all four into a fake robot main loop that runs ten times, printing sense, decide and act each cycle. That printout is module 1 in code.
modules.whyItWorks: Robot code is not exotic. It is variables holding sensor readings, loops running the control cycle, if statements choosing behaviour, and functions keeping it readable. Writing it on paper first is what professionals do when hardware time is expensive — and a shared phone is expensive time.
modules.challenge: Write a function that takes a list of sensor readings and returns the average. Then use it to smooth ten noisy numbers. Noisy sensors are the normal case, not the exception.

words.means: a named place that holds a value you can change
a reusable named block of code that can take inputs
code that only runs when a test is true

modules.title: Simulate the Robot
modules.bigIdea: A simulator lets you crash a thousand times for free before you touch real hardware.

seeThis.caption: A simulated robot following a black line around a curve on a phone screen.

youNeed: the shared phone with a free browser robot simulator or block-and-Python robot environment
your control loop diagram from module 1
paper for logging results
doThis: Set up a line-following task. Before writing anything, name your sensor, your decision and your action out loud.
Write the crudest possible controller: if the sensor sees dark, turn one way; otherwise turn the other. Run it.
Watch it wobble violently down the line. That wobble is the signature of on-off control — point at it, it is important.
Log the time to complete the course. Then double the turn amount and log again. Then halve it. Three numbers, one table.
Add a straight-ahead zone: only turn if the sensor is strongly one way. The wobble should shrink. Log the time again.
Now break it on purpose: add a sharp corner it cannot handle, and write down exactly why it fails.
modules.whyItWorks: On-off control, also called bang-bang control, is the simplest thing that works and it is genuinely used where the wobble does not matter — a fridge thermostat, for instance. But on a moving robot it wastes energy and overshoots constantly. Feeling that limitation yourself is what makes the next module land.
modules.challenge: Beat your best lap time by changing only ONE number per run, logging every attempt. Bring your table to module 6 — you will need it.

words.means: a controller with only full-on and full-off outputs
going past the target before correcting back
a model of the real system you can test against safely

modules.title: Proportional Control, No Panic
modules.bigIdea: Correct in proportion to how wrong you are — small error, small nudge; big error, big shove.

seeThis.caption: Two traces side by side: one wobbling wildly, one settling smoothly onto the line.

youNeed: the simulator from module 5, still set up
your logged table of times
paper for a tuning table
doThis: Define error properly: how far the sensor reading is from where you want it. Write that one line of code first, and print it.
Replace your on-off rule with: correction = Kp * error. Start with a small Kp. Run it.
Log three columns for every run: Kp, lap time, and how much it wobbled from one to five.
Raise Kp steadily. At some point the robot starts oscillating and never settles. Write down that Kp — you have found the point of instability yourself.
Now drop Kp too low. It drifts off the line lazily and misses corners. Note that number too. Good tuning lives between your two failures.
Pick your best Kp and run it three times to prove it was not luck. Then explain, in one sentence, what Kp physically means.
modules.whyItWorks: The P in PID is proportional control, and on many real systems it is enough on its own. Too little gain and the system is sluggish; too much and it oscillates — exactly what you measured. The I and D terms exist to fix two specific leftover problems, steady offset and overshoot, but tuning always starts here, and it always starts with finding the two failure points.
modules.challenge: Add a D term: subtract a small multiple of how fast the error is changing. Retune and see whether you can push Kp higher without oscillation. That is damping, and you can feel it working.

words.means: the difference between where you are and where you want to be
the multiplier that turns error into correction, often called Kp
swinging back and forth past the target without settling

modules.title: Wire It, Then Drive It
modules.bigIdea: A servo does not spin freely — you tell it an angle, and it holds that angle against the world.

seeThis.caption: A small servo horn swinging between three chalk-marked angles on a board.

youNeed: one cheap hobby servo (SG90 class) and a microcontroller board if you can borrow or share one; otherwise a DC motor salvaged from a broken toy
a battery holder with AA cells, wire, tape and a screwdriver
cardboard or scrap wood for a mount, and an adult present for any cutting or soldering
doThis: SAFETY: low-voltage batteries only — never mains, never a car battery, never a cut charging cable. Do not power a servo directly from a microcontroller's pin if it stalls; give motors their own battery and join the grounds.
Mount the servo firmly to cardboard or wood first. An unmounted servo just shakes itself around and teaches you nothing.
Send it to 0 degrees, then 90, then 180, pausing between. Mark each position in chalk on the board beneath the horn. Those three marks are your proof it obeys.
Now push gently against the horn while it is holding position. Feel it push back. That resistance is a control loop running inside the servo, and it is module 1 in your hand.
Write a function arm_to(angle) that moves it and waits. Then loop through a list of angles. Reuse, do not retype.

Salvage route without a board: run a DC motor from batteries, swap the wires to reverse it, and use your module 3 knowledge to pulse the connection by hand — count your on-time and off-time out loud and watch the speed change.
modules.whyItWorks: Inside every hobby servo is a tiny closed loop: a potentiometer measures the actual shaft angle, compares it to the commanded angle, and drives the motor until the error is zero. That is why it pushes back when you shove it. You spent five modules learning that loop; now you can feel it resisting your thumb.
modules.challenge: Measure the servo's real limits. Find the smallest angle change it reliably makes, and the heaviest load it can hold before it gives up. Write both numbers on the mount.

words.means: a motor that moves to and holds a commanded angle
any component that turns a signal into physical movement
the shared reference wire that all parts of a circuit must connect to

modules.title: Capstone: The Sorting Arm
modules.bigIdea: Build a machine that sees a decision, acts on it and repeats — and prove it with numbers and a photograph.

seeThis.caption: A servo arm on a cardboard base flicking grains into one of two tins, with a phone propped up filming it.

youNeed: your servo or motor rig from module 7, mounted
a chute or ramp, two tins, and material to sort: maize grains, beans, bottle caps
the shared phone for code and one photo or short video
doThis: Draw the state machine FIRST, on paper, the way you learned in module 2: WAITING, DECIDING, SORTING LEFT, SORTING RIGHT, back to WAITING.
Build the physical path: a chute that delivers one item at a time to the arm's reach. Getting one item at a time is harder than the code and you should expect to redesign it twice.
Write the control code as one loop with a function per state. Keep each function short enough to read on a phone screen without scrolling.
For version one, you are the sensor: press a key for good or bad and let the arm act. Separating deciding from acting is a design choice, not a shortcut.
Run 30 items. Record: how many were correctly placed, how many jammed, and the total time. Three honest numbers.

Fix the single biggest failure, run 30 again, and put the two result sets side by side. Then photograph the rig with your state diagram and code beside it, and explain the whole thing to someone in under two minutes.
modules.whyItWorks: You have now built a complete cyber-physical system: a state machine, a control loop, an actuator, a mechanical feed and a measured evaluation. Industrial grain and coffee sorters differ from yours in speed and in having a camera where you stood, but the architecture on the whiteboard is the same one you drew on paper. Jams, incidentally, are where real sorting machines actually spend their engineering budget.
modules.challenge: Replace yourself as the sensor. Use the phone camera and your classifier work, or a simple light sensor, so the machine decides for itself. Then measure how much worse it is than you — and be honest about the number.

words.means: a system where software and moving hardware control each other
how many items a machine can handle per minute
one round of build, measure, improve

courses.title: Drone Tech & Flight
courses.tagline: Four forces, three axes, one set of laws you must not break.
courses.intro: Drones are a serious tool in Africa right now — carrying medical supplies, surveying farmland, mapping after floods. This course treats you like a future operator: you will learn the physics properly, learn the law properly, plan real missions, measure real thrust, and produce a survey report you could hand to somebody.
courses.parentNote: Your teenager will learn the aerodynamics, control axes, mission planning and — crucially — the genuine regulatory and safety obligations of drone flight, without needing a drone. The capstone is a planned, executed and written-up aerial survey of a real site using only a phone and a raised camera position.

modules.title: Four Forces, Measured
modules.bigIdea: Flight is a permanent argument between four forces, and you can measure every one of them.

seeThis.caption: A cardboard aircraft shape on the ground with four labelled sticks pointing out from its centre.

youNeed: a length of elastic or rubber bands, string, and a bag or tin
stones as known weights, and a ruler or marked stick
a piece of cardboard and a flat open area
doThis: Make a scale: hang the elastic from a branch, attach a tin, add stones one at a time and mark the stretch each time. You now have a force meter in units of stones.
Weigh a cardboard sheet with it. That is weight, and it never changes direction — always straight down toward the Earth's centre.
Now hold the cardboard flat and run, then hold it edge-on and run. Same object, hugely different push. That difference is drag, and it depends on the area facing the airflow.
Tie the cardboard to the elastic and pull it through the air at a steady speed. Read the stretch. You have measured drag as a number.
Repeat at double the speed. Note that the stretch grows much more than double — drag rises far faster than speed does. That single fact governs the range of every aircraft.
Draw all four force arrows on your cardboard, sized to your measurements. Then state the hover condition in one line: lift equals weight, thrust equals drag.
modules.whyItWorks: A hovering drone is not doing nothing; it is holding lift exactly equal to weight while burning battery. Because drag climbs steeply with speed, flying fast is disproportionately expensive, which is why delivery drones cruise at an efficient speed rather than a maximum one. Every payload gram you add must be paid for in lift, and lift is paid for in battery.
modules.challenge: Build two cardboard shapes with identical weight but very different drag. Measure both, then predict which would fly further on the same battery and justify it with your numbers.

words.means: the upward force generated by pushing air downward
the resistance of air against a moving body, rising steeply with speed
the useful weight carried, such as a camera or medical supplies

modules.title: Yaw, Pitch, Roll
modules.bigIdea: Every possible movement of a flying machine is a mix of three rotations and three slides.

seeThis.caption: A cardboard X-frame held in two hands, tipping nose-down, then leaning sideways, then spinning flat.

youNeed: two strips of cardboard taped into an X, with a marked nose
a marker or charcoal to label the arms
space to stand and turn
doThis: Build the X-frame and mark one arm clearly as the NOSE. Orientation is meaningless without a nose.
