Hold it level. Now spin it flat, like a plate on a table, nose sweeping the horizon. That is yaw.
Tip the nose down and up. That is pitch, and it is what makes a quadcopter move forward and back.
Lean it left and right, like tipping a bowl. That is roll, and it moves the craft sideways.
Now the key insight: a quadcopter has no wings and no rudder. It pitches forward by spinning the two rear motors faster. Point at the two arms that speed up as you pitch the frame.
Combine: pitch forward and yaw at the same time and watch how quickly you lose track of which arm is the nose. That confusion is the single most common cause of crashes.
modules.whyItWorks: A quadcopter controls all six degrees of freedom using only four numbers: the speed of each motor. Pitch and roll come from differences between opposite pairs; yaw comes from the difference between the two diagonal pairs; total thrust comes from all four together. That is why a flight controller does arithmetic hundreds of times a second — it is constantly translating your stick movements into four motor speeds.
modules.challenge: Work out which motors speed up and which slow down for each of the four commands: climb, pitch forward, roll right, yaw left. Write it as a table and defend it.

words.means: rotation about the vertical axis — changing which way the nose points
rotation nose-up or nose-down
rotation leaning left or right

modules.title: Why Two Spin Backwards
modules.bigIdea: Spinning a propeller one way twists the whole aircraft the other way — so half of them must spin in reverse.

seeThis.caption: A quadcopter frame drawn in chalk with curved arrows: diagonally opposite arms turning the same way.

youNeed: a bicycle wheel if you can borrow one, or a heavy stone on a long string
a chair that spins, or a smooth patch of ground you can pivot on
a friend to observe and record
doThis: Stand on a smooth spot holding a stone on a string. Swing it around your head one way. Feel yourself being twisted the other way.
Swap direction. Feel the twist reverse. That is Newton's third law working on rotation, and you can feel it in your feet.
If you have a bicycle wheel and a spinning chair: hold the spinning wheel and tilt it. You will turn. Have your friend film it, because nobody believes it the first time.
Now draw a quadcopter and put clockwise arrows on all four propellers. Ask: which way does the body twist? Write your answer.
Redraw it with diagonally opposite pairs spinning opposite ways. The twists now cancel. Point at the cancelling pairs.
Last question, and it is the good one: if all four cancel exactly, how does a drone yaw deliberately? Work it out before reading the next paragraph.
modules.whyItWorks: The answer is that it unbalances the cancellation on purpose: speed up one diagonal pair and slow the other, keeping total thrust the same, and the leftover reaction torque rotates the aircraft. This is also why a single-rotor helicopter needs a tail rotor — without it, the fuselage would simply spin the other way. And it is why propellers are sold in matched clockwise and counter-clockwise pairs; fitting the wrong one is a guaranteed crash.
modules.challenge: Explain to someone who has never flown anything why a helicopter has a small tail rotor, using only your stone-on-a-string demonstration. If they get it, you understand it.

words.means: a twisting force
the equal and opposite force that always accompanies a force
pairs of propellers spinning in opposite directions to cancel torque

modules.title: Fly the Simulator
modules.bigIdea: The skill of flying is almost entirely the skill of knowing which way the nose is pointing.

seeThis.caption: A phone in landscape showing a quadcopter hovering, seen from behind, with two virtual sticks.

youNeed: the shared phone with a free flight simulator in the browser or as an app
twenty uninterrupted minutes and a stable surface
paper to record times and mistakes
doThis: Hover only, for two full minutes, without drifting more than a body-width. Time it. Most people cannot do it first try.
Practise climb and descend while holding position. Note that descending is harder — the craft settles into its own disturbed air.
Fly a box pattern nose-forward, turning at each corner so the nose always leads. Log your time.
Now fly the same box with the nose locked toward you the entire time. Your left and right are now reversed. This is the single skill that separates pilots from crashers.
Practise a deliberate emergency: kill throttle, then recover before impact. Do it ten times. It costs nothing here and it costs everything in real life.
Finally, fly a straight survey line at constant height and constant speed, twice. Compare your two runs — consistency, not flair, is what mapping needs.
modules.whyItWorks: Reversed controls when the aircraft faces you cause a large share of beginner crashes, and simulator hours are the standard, cheap fix used by professionals worldwide. The constant-height, constant-speed line you practised last is the actual working skill for aerial survey, where a wobbling flight path ruins the photo overlap and the map with it.
modules.challenge: Fly the box pattern nose-in with your eyes on the aircraft, not the sticks, and beat your previous time. Then teach a friend the reversal trick in one sentence.

words.means: knowing which way the aircraft's nose is pointing relative to you
the aircraft's angle in the air — its pitch, roll and yaw at a moment
the control setting total motor power and therefore climb or descent

modules.title: Airspace, Law and Responsibility
modules.bigIdea: Flying legally is a professional skill, and in most countries flying illegally is a criminal matter, not a telling-off.

seeThis.caption: A checklist board with three red-crossed icons: airport, private property, crowds.

youNeed: the shared phone with internet to find your country's actual rules
paper to write a real pre-flight checklist
an adult or teacher to review your findings
doThis: Find your own country's civil aviation authority website and locate its drone or RPAS page. Do not rely on anything you were told secondhand, including this course — check the source.

Write down the answers to five questions: must the drone be registered, must the operator be licensed or permitted, what is the maximum height allowed, how far must you stay from an airport, and is flying over people allowed.

Note the pattern you will find across many African countries — Kenya, Nigeria, Ghana, Rwanda, South Africa and others require registration and prior authorisation, with penalties for flying without it, and rules differ enough between countries that you must always check locally.
Learn the two universals: never fly near an airport or approach path, and always keep the aircraft in your direct line of sight.
Now the human side. Write down who you would need to ask before flying over a neighbour's compound, a market, a school or a funeral — and what you would say to them.
Build a pre-flight checklist of ten items covering aircraft, battery, weather, people and permission. Sign and date it. That is what a professional operator actually carries.
modules.whyItWorks: Drones do genuinely valuable work across Africa — delivering blood and medical supplies to hard-to-reach clinics, surveying farmland, and assessing damage after floods — and that work exists only because operators are trusted and regulated. Regulators respond to incidents, so a single reckless flight near an airport affects the rules for everyone. Knowing the law is not bureaucracy; it is the price of being allowed to do the interesting work.
modules.challenge: Write a one-page permission request to a real landowner for a real survey: what you will fly, when, over what, what you will do with the images, and how you will protect their privacy. Show it to an adult and take their criticism seriously.

words.means: remotely piloted aircraft system, the formal legal term for a drone
the requirement to keep the aircraft visible to your own eyes
official permission to fly, required in many countries before every flight or class of flight

modules.title: Plan a Real Mission
modules.bigIdea: A good aerial map is decided before takeoff, in the numbers you choose for height, spacing and overlap.

seeThis.caption: A boustrophedon flight path drawn over a field outline, lines running back and forth like ploughing.

youNeed: the shared phone with a map app or satellite view of a real area
paper, ruler and pen for the flight plan
a real site: a school field, a farm plot, a market ground
doThis: Choose a real site and sketch its outline. Measure its rough size by pacing it out and counting your steps — then convert steps to metres.

Understand the core trade: fly low and each photo covers little ground but shows fine detail; fly high and you cover ground fast but see less. The size of ground each pixel represents is called ground sample distance.
Decide your detail requirement first. If you must see individual maize plants, you must fly low, and that decision fixes everything else.

Draw your flight lines back and forth across the site, spaced so that neighbouring strips overlap sideways by roughly 60 to 70 percent, with even more overlap along each line. Generous overlap is what makes stitching work.

Count the photos your plan needs and estimate the flight time. Compare that to a realistic battery endurance of roughly 20 to 30 minutes for a typical small survey drone. If your plan does not fit, split it into two flights — do not shave the overlap.
Add the non-flying columns: takeoff and landing spot, wind direction, who has been informed, and where people will be kept back. A plan without those is not a plan.
modules.whyItWorks: Insufficient overlap is the classic beginner failure: the software cannot find enough matching points between photos and the map comes out torn or warped. Because coverage, detail and battery all pull against each other, the professional habit is to fix the detail requirement first and let it drive the rest. Planning on paper also forces the safety questions to be answered before anyone is standing in a field with a spinning aircraft.
modules.challenge: Plan the same site twice: once for maximum detail and once for minimum flight time. Present both plans with photo counts and time estimates, and recommend one with a reason.

words.means: how much real ground each pixel of the image covers
the fraction of ground shared between neighbouring photos, needed for stitching
how long the aircraft can stay airborne on one battery

modules.title: Build a Thrust Test Rig
modules.bigIdea: Thrust-to-weight ratio decides whether an aircraft flies well, flies badly, or does not fly at all.

seeThis.caption: A motor and propeller mounted on one end of a pivoted beam, balanced against stones on the other.

youNeed: a small DC motor salvaged from a broken toy, fan or drone, plus batteries and wire
a light stiff beam, a pivot, string, and small stones or coins as calibrated weights
a propeller cut from a plastic bottle or stiff paper, plus eye protection and an adult supervising
doThis: SAFETY, and this one is not optional: propellers cause real injuries. Use paper or thin plastic blades, never metal. Protect your eyes, clamp the rig down, keep everyone to the side and never in the plane of the disc, and disconnect the battery before touching anything.
Calibrate your weights first. Find something of known mass and compare, or at minimum use identical coins so your unit is consistent. Uncalibrated results are just opinions.
Mount the motor at one end of the beam blowing downwards, pivot in the middle, weight pan at the other end. Measure both arm lengths — if they differ, your reading is scaled by that ratio.
Run the motor and add weights until the beam balances level. Record the thrust in your chosen units.

Vary one thing at a time: blade twist, blade length, battery voltage. Build a table with at least six rows. Longer blades and more twist generally give more thrust but draw more current and can stall the motor — watch for the motor bogging down.

Now compute the ratio that matters. Estimate the mass of a hypothetical aircraft using four of your motors, and work out total thrust divided by weight. Anything at or below 1 cannot leave the ground; controllable flight generally wants roughly 2 or more.
modules.whyItWorks: A thrust-to-weight ratio of exactly 1 means the aircraft can hover only at full throttle, with nothing left for correcting a gust — which means it is uncontrollable. Real designs keep spare thrust in hand, and that headroom is what lets the flight controller make the constant tiny corrections you practised in module 4. Your table of blade twist versus thrust is a genuine propeller characterisation, done the same way in a lab with a load cell instead of stones.
modules.challenge: Find the point of diminishing returns: keep increasing blade area until thrust stops rising and the motor starts labouring. Record the current draw if you can borrow a meter, and explain what is happening.

words.means: total thrust divided by total weight, which must exceed 1 to fly
measuring how a component performs across a range of conditions
when a motor or blade is loaded past the point where it can perform

modules.title: Capstone: The Aerial Survey Report
modules.bigIdea: Plan, fly, map and report a real site — and deliver something a real person could act on.

seeThis.caption: A finished survey report on a board: site plan, stitched photo map, findings list and safety checklist, photographed together.

youNeed: your mission plan from module 6 and checklist from module 5
the shared phone and a raised camera position: a long pole, a safe roof with an adult, or a kite or balloon if you have one
card, tape and pen for the report, and permission from whoever controls the site
doThis: Get permission first, in the words you drafted in module 5, from whoever actually controls the site. No permission, no survey — this is the part professionals never skip.
Execute your plan: fixed height, straight lines, consistent overlap, photos pointing straight down. If conditions change halfway — light, wind, dust — note it, because it will show in your images.
Stitch your images into one map. Free stitching software or careful manual overlapping on card both work; state honestly which you used.

Analyse the map for findings a person could act on: where water pools, which section of a plot is thinner, where a path has worn through, how much unused ground there is. Aim for three findings, each with an arrow and a sentence.

Quantify at least one finding. Use a known object in frame — a doorway, a step length, a jerry can — as a scale reference, and estimate an area or a distance. State your uncertainty; a range is more honest than a single number.

Assemble the report: site and permission, method with height and overlap, the map, three findings, limitations, and your signed safety checklist. Photograph it. Then present it to the person who controls the site and write down their response on the back.
modules.whyItWorks: This is the actual deliverable of the drone survey industry. Nobody pays for photographs; they pay for findings they can act on, backed by a stated method and honest limits. By doing it with a pole and a phone you have practised every part that is hard — permission, planning, consistency, stitching, analysis and reporting — and left out only the part that is bought with money.
modules.challenge: Survey the same site again after a change: after rain, after harvest, after a month. Produce a comparison report showing what moved, and let the two maps make the argument for you.

words.means: a single map image stitched from many overlapping aerial photos
checking on foot what the aerial image seems to show
the finished product handed to whoever needed the work done
